one_liner: Header-only C++17 machine learning library (Armadillo-based) whose tree-based k-NN and k-means beat 2012-era scikit-learn, Shogun, MATLAB and Weka.
what_it_does: A broad classical-ML toolkit (nearest-neighbor and range search, k-means, GMMs, HMMs, LARS, decision trees, random forests, a neural-network module and more) written as C++ templates over Armadillo matrices, with generated CLI, Python, R, Julia and Go bindings. It is not a drop-in for scikit-learn: the C++ API is class-based (e.g. KNN knn(referenceSet); knn.Search(k, neighbors, distances); KMeans<>().Cluster(data, k, assignments)) on column-major arma::mat data, and behaviour such as tree type, distance metric or Lloyd-step algorithm is chosen through template parameters.
how_it_is_fast: k-NN uses space-partitioning trees (kd-tree by default; cover trees, ball trees, R-trees and spill trees available) with the tree-independent dual-tree algorithm, which prunes query-node/reference-node pairs at once instead of searching point by point. Policy-based templates resolve distance metrics and tree types at compile time, and Armadillo expression templates avoid temporary copies. k-means offers Elkan, Hamerly, Pelleg-Moore and dual-tree Lloyd steps besides the naive OpenMP-parallel step, which is the default.
when_to_use: Exact all-k-nearest-neighbor or range search on low-to-moderate dimensional data (tens of dimensions) with up to millions of points, from C++ without a Python runtime.
C++ deployment where you want header-only code with no runtime beyond Armadillo plus a BLAS/LAPACK, and the option to expose the same model to Python, R, Julia or Go.
k-means with a fixed set of starting centroids where you can choose an accelerated Lloyd step (HamerlyKMeans, ElkanKMeans, DualTreeKMeans) by template parameter.
Research or prototyping that needs swappable distance metrics, tree types or approximation (epsilon) levels without writing new search code.
when_not_to_use: High-dimensional nearest-neighbor search (hundreds of dimensions or more): trees degrade, the docs point to NAIVE mode for that case, and approximate libraries such as FAISS scale further; even in the 2013 table mnist (784 dimensions) took mlpack 2719.8 s.
When you want a drop-in acceleration of existing scikit-learn code: the API, data layout (column-major, one point per column) and model objects differ.
Multi-core k-NN: the neighbor-search code contains no OpenMP, so a single search runs on one thread; only some methods (naive k-means, final k-means assignment) parallelise internally.
Deep learning at scale or GPU work: the neural-network module is CPU/Armadillo based and nothing here was benchmarked against PyTorch or TensorFlow.
Projects sensitive to build time: the README warns that the template-heavy code makes compilation slow unless individual headers and extern templates are used.

integration.dependencies: Armadillo >= 10.8 (with BLAS and LAPACK), ensmallen >= 2.10.0, cereal >= 1.1.2; bundles STB (images), cpp-httplib (dataset download) and dr_libs (audio), each switchable to system copies or disabled by macros in config.hpp
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; CMake 3.19 for the build and tests; GCC 8+ (CMake check), clang 3.5+, MSVC with /bigobj
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows (vcpkg or source build); docs cover cross-compiling to ARMv7 (Raspberry Pi 2)
integration.thread_safety: not documented for sharing one KNN or KMeans object across threads; compile with -fopenmp for the internally parallel methods, and a thread-specific random seed bug was fixed in 4.7.0 (#4027)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same algorithms as scikit-learn, but a C++ API (or mlpack's own Python bindings) with different classes, parameters and column-major data layout; existing sklearn code must be rewritten

gotchas: The headline benchmark is not settings-matched and is unstable across the authors' own papers: on the same AMD Phenom II X6 1100T, a uniform 1,000,000 x 10 all-k-NN took scikit-learn 1550.720 s against mlpack's 1423.949 s (about 1.09x, k=5, CSV load and save included) in the 2011 mlpack paper, but 8780.0176 s against 1020.9142 s (about 8.6x, k=3, load excluded) in the 2013 JMLR table; scikit-learn's version and search algorithm are stated in neither, so the large ratios depend on an undocumented competitor configuration (derived from page data).

In the 2013 k-means table scikit-learn 'ran out of memory' from miniboone (130,064 x 50, 2 clusters, about 52 MB as doubles, derived from page data) upward on an 8 GB machine, which points to a harness or version problem rather than an algorithmic limit; those six rows are failures, not timings.

KMeans<> defaults to NaiveKMeans (a per-point distance loop, not a BLAS matrix product); the accelerated Elkan, Hamerly, Pelleg-Moore and dual-tree steps must be selected as the LloydStepType template argument. Issue #4155 (May 2026) measured cover-tree k-NN 3-8x slower than the Beygelzimer reference implementation, with covtype tree construction 26x slower and dual-tree mode slower than single-tree on some data sets; 4.8.0 lists a 5-10x cover-tree construction speedup (#4164).

KNN copies the reference set unless it is passed with std::move, the tree build reorders points (indices are mapped back), a reused query tree must be reset with ResetTree() between searches, and OpenBLAS 0.3.26 or older built with pthreads oversubscribes threads when combined with -fopenmp (README warning).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick mlpack over oneDAL/sklearnex when you are writing C++ (not Python) and want exact tree-based neighbor search or swappable k-means variants in a header-only package; pick oneDAL to accelerate existing scikit-learn code in place, and FAISS when vectors are high-dimensional, the data set is huge or approximate search on GPU is acceptable.
verified_claims_summary: The JMLR 2013 MLOSS paper by mlpack's own authors timed mlpack 1.0.3 against 2012-era scikit-learn, Shogun, MATLAB, Weka and mlpy (versions, compiler and flags not stated) on one AMD Phenom II X6 1100T with 8 GB RAM, mean of 5 runs, load time excluded: all-k-NN with k=3 ran, for example, 20.2 s vs scikit-learn's 714.2 s on miniboone (about 35x) and 1020.9 s vs 8780.0 s on a 1,000,000 x 10 uniform set, and k-means from shared starting centroids ran 727.1 s vs MATLAB's 3117.5 s and Shogun's 7443.3 s on that set, with scikit-learn out of memory. An independent HPDC 2017 knor paper reportedly found mlpack and scikit-learn at parity per k-means iteration on Friendster-8 (13.09 s vs 12.84 s, single-threaded; search snippet only, paper not opened).
status_note: Actively maintained (4.8.0 released 2026-06-07 with further changes already queued in HISTORY.md, NumFOCUS-sponsored, BSD-3-Clause, 5.7k stars) and copyable as headers, but its speed evidence is a 2013 self-run comparison whose competitor settings are unstated and inconsistent with the authors' 2011 run, so re-benchmark against current scikit-learn before relying on the ratios.
